kept.excerpt: U.S. forces ended the seventh consecutive night of strikes against Iran on July 17 at 9:30 p.m. ET. U.S. forces employed fighter aircraft, aerial drones, and warships in addition to other assets. CENTCOM continues to hold Iran accountable at the Commander in Chief's direction while fully enforcing a naval blockade against Iranian ports.
kept.relevance: This near-cutoff official statement establishes active warship operations and blockade enforcement, but does not confirm passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

kept.excerpt: More than 20 U.S. warships, depicted in the graphic above, are operating in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, along with hundreds of aircraft dispersed across various bases, vessels, and forward arming and refueling points in the Middle East. Amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, dock landing ship USS Comstock, and amphibious transport dock USS Portland sailed into U.S. 5th Fleet in early July.
kept.relevance: The regional force inventory identifies available military vessels, including amphibious ships, while their reported operating areas alone do not establish a qualifying transit.

kept.excerpt: “U.S. forces resumed the naval blockade against vessels transiting to and from Iranian ports and coastal areas today at 4 p.m. ET,” U.S. Central Command said in an online statement Tuesday. “There are currently more than 20 U.S. Navy warships and hundreds of military aircraft operating across the Middle East.” Prior to announcing the reinstatement of its blockade, the U.S. had urged ships to use a southern route that hugs the coast of Oman.
kept.publisher: NPR, republished by KPBS Public Media
kept.relevance: This dated report confirms implementation of the blockade and describes the U.S.-promoted route near Oman, providing operational context without treating commercial movements as warship transits.

kept.excerpt: At the Commander in Chief's direction, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces will resume blockading maritime traffic entering and exiting Iranian ports on July 14 at 4 p.m. ET. CENTCOM forces will enforce the blockade against vessels transiting to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas. All mariners are advised to monitor Notice to Mariners broadcasts and contact U.S. naval forces on bridge-to-bridge channel 16 when operating in the Gulf of Oman and Strait of Hormuz approaches.
kept.relevance: The official announcement supplies a concrete operational start time and geographic context, but activity in the approaches does not independently satisfy the narrowest-section requirement.

kept.excerpt: “The blockade will not impede neutral transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations. Neutral vessels may still be subject to the right of visit and search to determine the presence of contraband cargo or to ensure they are not intending to breach the blockade,” reads the notice. The U.S. and Iran continue to have dueling routes through the Strait, with Iran relying on its so-called Tehran toll passage while the U.S. promotes the path closer to Oman, although it comes with the risk of Iranian attacks.
kept.relevance: The report details the maritime enforcement notice and competing routes, clarifying the operational setting and risks relevant to possible military passage.

kept.excerpt: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) completed a third round of strikes this week against Iran, July 11, holding Iranian forces accountable for attacking another commercial ship in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. forces hit approximately 140 Iranian military targets with precision munitions launched by land- and sea-based fighter aircraft, drones, and naval vessels. Since early May, U.S. forces have helped facilitate the successful transit of more than 800 commercial vessels and 400 million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
kept.relevance: The statement documents naval participation and the shipping-protection mission, while its commercial-transit figures cannot be counted as qualifying military transits.
